rationale: This qualitative study (based on 20 key informant interviews, focus group discussions with gaon samaj leaders, qualitative pipeline mapping, and archival/document review) compares centralized municipal utility provision in Darjeeling with decentralized private for-profit water markets (tankers/handcarts) and community-managed collective systems (gaon samaj). Because the analysis co-equally centers on municipal versus private/community utility ownership and management models (regulatory_model_ownership), decentralized governance, core-periphery jurisdictional/mandate gaps, and lack of municipal-samaj coordination (institutional_structure_coordination), and community water collectives/participatory inclusion (participation_assistance), with secondary discussion of flat municipal water taxes, samaj dues, and tanker pricing (fees_tariffs_subsidies), primary_mechanism_family is regulatory_model_ownership and assigned_mechanism_label_with_multiple is multiple. On the outcome side, effective_access (water scarcity/quantity, pipe leakage, alternate-day reliability, potability/contamination, and physical fetching/queuing burdens) is primary alongside co-central analysis of municipal network connection exclusions on the town periphery (primary_connection) and household affordability burdens from expensive tanker water (economic_access), warranting multiple for assigned_outcome_label_with_multiple.
